Alright, let's break out some equations.

The median lethal dose of water is 6L. Assuming that you have 6L of water at 0C, what would it do to the human body temperature?

H = m * C * T, where H = total heat, m = mass, C = specific heat, and T = temperature. Energy is conserved, so the loss of heat in the body should equal the rise in heat of the ice. So

mi * Ci * (T - Ti) = mb * Cb * (Tb - T)

The mass of 6L of water is 6kg. The specific heat of ice is 2.108 kJ/kgK. The initial temperature is 0C. For the body, the average mass of a person is about 80kg. Average specific heat is 3.47kJ/kgK, and initial temperature is 37C. Plugging that in gives us

6 * 2.108 * (T - 0) = 80 * 3.47 * (37 - T)

Solving for T gives T = 35.4C.

The interesting thing here is that hypothermia sets in when core temperature stays below 35C for a period of time. That's pretty close to the resulting temperature. Your body would be working to bring that up, so it shouldn't stay there very long. Given that you're ingesting the ice cubes, you can imagine that it would have more of an impact on your core than it would, say, your leg. But the body also has a pretty great heat distribution system in the circulatory system. You're also nearing the limit of the capacity of the human stomach, which is about 4L.

All things considered, assuming you're not urinating, I'm calling the water toxicity kills you first. But I can't say with any certainty.

OS X, because it has great gui apps and it's Unix. As a developer-architect I do full-stack development as well as corporate presentations to aid the sales people, when the customer needs technical explanations. I do some windows-browser testing in Parallels virtual machines. Linux doesn't add any benefits as an development environment, but I deploy the apps on Linux servers, where it has a cost benefit and the benefit of the option of trimming down the distro to the bare minimum of what's absolutely necessary to run the app.
OS X here with VirtualBox for testing and Ubuntu for my servers.

My team uses a cross-platform IDE (PhpStorm) and virtual Ubuntu dev servers (Vagrant + VirtualBox). I do a lot of cross-browser testing with BrowserStack, which lets me control VMs remotely and runs in my local browser.

With a setup like that, my OS doesn't really matter anymore. I have a Windows 7 desktop at my office but use a MacBook Pro with OS X at home. Both work great. It really all comes down to what you're more comfortable using for general stuff. Personally I prefer font rendering and the overall UI of Mac OS. Plus I spend a lot of time on the command line and would rather do it in BASH than a Windows shell. But it doesn't make a big difference at the end of the day.

I'm using Linux - KDE 5 on Manjaro for my development environment (Python primarily) with Ubuntu and Debian on the server side. I have OSX and Windows too, but don't do dev work on those. Used Kubuntu on the desktop for years but recently moved to Manjaro for various reasons.

I could probably use OSX almost as easily, but only one of my machines will run that, and I wouldn't gain anything anyway. For me, the advantage is that I can run the server side stuff just as easily on a desktop machine. LXC and other such technologies mean I can wind up a server instance on my desktop in seconds (similar to FreeBSD Jails, virtualisation without the overhead) and all the Python stuff is readily available, everything automatically updates, etc ... And KDE Plasma 5 is a fantastic desktop, really nice to use, although it's still having a few growing pains at the moment. (nothing like the early KDE 4 days though)
